transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Shaw (Redwood AE), Priya Kaur (Redwood SE), Dana Morales (Medora Head of ML), Liam O'Connor (Infra), Sofia Park (Product)

Summary:
- Review of latest bench runs comparing Redwood to incumbent provider (latency and throughput).
- Identified tail-latency spikes at p99 for long prompts; batching and KV cache settings discussed.
- Agreement to run dedicated slot stress test and A/B quantization runs.
- Next steps: data share, dedicated slot scheduling, VPC peering, and success criteria confirmation.

Topics: benchmark results, routing policy, quantization, KV cache, dedicated slots, VPC/connectivity, SOC2 questions

Transcript body:
[00:00] Ethan: okay hi everyone, thanks for joining, we have about 40ish minutes, i'll jump straight into the numbers from the lab runs this week — sha- Priya you wanna take the slides?
[00:14] Priya: yeah i'll share, um, quick note, a couple of names might be munged in the auto-header, so if anything's wrong say so.
[00:21] Dana: all good, you can call me Dana.
[00:24] Priya: cool, so high level, we ran the same model family you gave us earlier (we used the 13B variant you asked for) on both Redwood-hosted and on the incumbent vendor's reserved endpoint. we matched the sequence length distribution to your prod samples (majority 128 tokens, 20% long tails ~512).
[00:40] Priya: baseline (IncumbentVendor) p50 72ms p95 210ms p99 860ms throughput 320 reqs/min under 4 gpu pool.
[00:51] Priya: Redwood-hosted default route p50 68ms p95 170ms p99 420ms throughput 335 reqs/min. note p99 is a big win but we still saw spikes with long prompts.
[01:06] Sofia: sorry can i interrupt, what's your test harness — are these synthetic prompts or replayed with user context?
[01:12] Priya: good call — these were a replay of anonymized traffic plus 1000 synthetic long-form prompts to stress the cache.
[01:21] Liam: interesting, the incumbent's p99 at 860ms is rough, that explains the user complaints. what did you configure for batching?
[01:27] Priya: we used continuous batching with a max batch window of 8ms and max batch size 16. We also enabled prefix KV cache for the short prompt set. the long prompts intentionally bypassed cache to simulate cold KV.
[01:40] Dana: when you say KV cache, is that the same as the key value cache in our runtime? i saw an email where it was called KV cash, so just checking.
[01:47] Ethan: yep it's KV cache — sometimes the transcript spells it cash — but it's the same thing.
[01:51] Dana: ok.
[01:53] Priya: we also tried a route that falls back to a slightly smaller quantized variant (q4_0) for tail requests — that reduced p99 but impacted some quality metrics a touch.
[02:05] Dana: how big of a quality hit? we care about hallucination rate and classification accuracy on short prompts.
[02:11] Priya: initial evals show BLEU-ish style deltas small, about 1.2% drop on the curated prompt set for the q4_0 variant versus the full fp16 baseline. for classification logits we saw near-identical top-1. we're going to run a larger safety/regression suite.
[02:29] Liam: curious about the dedicated option — if we move to Dedicated (reserved pool) can we get better tail latency?
[02:36] Ethan: yes, dedicated pools help because you avoid noisy neighbors and you can pin instance types and kernel selection. you'll see more predictable p95/p99 and higher sustained throughput because the scheduler is tuned to your traffic profile.
[02:50] Sofia: any ballpark on cost delta vs incumbent if we move to dedicated?
[02:54] Ethan: depends on commit level, but in our model we project roughly 15–25% premium over shared hosted for the reserved throughput we've modelled — though unit token cost can drop with batching and cache so net spend sometimes ends up similar. we'll send a more detailed delta in the CSV.
[03:12] Dana: on the long prompts noise — can we do smarter routing so long tails go to a quantized variant or to a dedicated slower lane?
[03:19] Priya: absolutely, routing policies can be set by prompt length, customer tier, or latency budget. you can route long tails to a cheaper quantized variant, to a dedicated slot, or even to a region with more capacity. there's an automatic fallback chain.
[03:33] Liam: what's the network set up for private deployment — if we do VPC peering will that change our latency numbers?
[03:40] Ethan: VPC peering reduces egress variability but add small extra hops. in most of our tests VPC peering improved tail-latency stability compared to public egress, especially when you have predictable path to the infra. but you need to test in your colo region.
[03:55] Dana: okay, also can you remind us on compliance — we need SOC2 and we need KMS/HSM integration, audit logs. the security reviewer will ask.
[04:04] Priya: Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS, HSM integrations, and audit logs; we also have SOC2 Type II docs and iso27001 in the packet. i'll attach the security pack but note the private mode is the one you'd choose if you need that full set.
[04:19] Sofia: when you say private mode is that the same as the 'on prem' product? we've got hybrid constraints.
[04:25] Ethan: there's Private (VPC-hosted control plane) and On-Prem (air gapped appliance) options. For hybrid, usually VPC peering plus dedicated pools gives the best tradeoff.
[04:36] Dana: cool.
[04:38] Priya: back to the numbers — we ran two additional experiments last night: 1) tighten batching window to 4ms and 2) pre-warm KV cache for long prompts.
[04:47] Priya: tighten window -> p95 improved by ~12% but throughput dropped ~8% under a burst. pre-warm KV -> p99 for long tails dropped from 420ms to ~260ms but requires a warmup traffic pattern or explicit prefetch.
[05:04] Liam: pre-warm sounds promising — would that be something we run at ingest time from our side?
[05:09] Priya: yes you can either send a prefetch phase or use our auto-prefetch policy that learns common prefixes and keeps them in cache. that increases costs slightly but really smooths the tail.
[05:20] Dana: what about model quantization experiments — you mentioned q4_0 and q8 — does Redwood recommend one over the other for our use case?
[05:28] Priya: for the 13B style family, q4_0 has the best p99/latency win with minimal quality impact; q8 tends to be smaller savings. but depends on exact prompt mix. we'll run A/B on your real prompts.
[05:40] Sofia: is there tooling to help us see token-level cost split by route/model? we need this for product planning.
[05:46] Ethan: yes the console has token-level cost breakdown, per-route and per-model charts. i'll give you a demo account so your product team can poke around.
[05:56] Dana: one more question on the benchmark — what version of the serving runtime and which kernels? we found earlier some providers used older kernels and that skewed results.
[06:04] Priya: good question — these runs used runtime 3.8.1 with nv_optimized kernels and an experimental attention kernel for long sequences. we'll include the kernel list in the CSV so you can compare apples-to-apples.
[06:16] Liam: any flags we should flip to reproduce the spikes? we want to run an internal sanity check.
[06:21] Priya: to reproduce the p99 spikes: disable prefix cache, increase sequence tail to 512+, and use a wide batching window. that tends to stress the KV and memory movement and shows the cold-path behavior.
[06:33] Dana: okay noted.
[06:36] Ethan: quick note about fallbacks — Redwood can fall back to a smaller model or a quantized variant automatically when latency climbs. that prevents errors but you may get slight quality drift, so you can tune thresholds.
[06:49] Sofia: do we have a recommended threshold for when to fallback? p95 above 250ms?
[06:54] Priya: typical threshold we've seen is p95 crossing 200–250ms for user-facing interactive apps. for high-throughput batch use cases you can be more lenient. we'll let you decide per-route.
[07:05] Dana: let's talk schedule: we want the dedicated stress test and the quantization A/B next week. can you stand up the 4 GPU pool and run peak-hour replay?
[07:14] Priya: yes we can provision a short reserved slot for a few hours (4xA100 equivalence). we'll coordinate with Liam for peering and credentials.
[07:22] Liam: i'll open a ticket for VPC peering and share creds by Monday.
[07:26] Ethan: cool — i'll share the CSV and the kernel list today. Priya will run the quantize A/B and drop results mid-next-week.
[07:34] Dana: sounds good. two administrative things — can we get incumbant vendor cost line items? we want to see total cost of ownership including data transfer.
[07:43] Ethan: we can approximate based on your usage profile and include transfer and storage. we'll label assumptions in the export.
[07:50] Sofia: and please flag any divergent measurement artifacts — e.g., different tokenization or pre/post processing — we need to ensure parity.
[07:58] Priya: yes we'll document tokenization, padding, EOS handling, and any model adapter changes.
[08:05] Dana: ok great, thanks everyone.

Recap (auto):
- Redwood shows meaningful tail improvement vs incumbent (p99 420ms vs 860ms) on hosted tests; additional tuning reduces p99 to ~260ms with pre-warm.
- Tradeoffs: quantization reduces latency but small quality delta; dedicated reserved pool increases predictability at a cost premium.
- Agreed experiments: Dedicated slot stress test, quantization A/B on real prompts, VPC peering test.

Explicit next steps (repeat):
- Ethan: share runs CSV + kernel list by EOD 2026-12-15.
- Priya: schedule Dedicated 4-GPU slot & run q4_0 vs fp16 A/B by 2026-12-19.
- Liam: provide VPC peering details and KMS thumbprint by 2026-12-20.
- Dana & Sofia: confirm success criteria by 2026-12-18.
